solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A song coming up — operatic piece

indicators.note: in a down entry, something coming up rises from the bottom, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: taken as written
an air is a simple tune or song

explanation.surface: A tune rising up the charts turns out to be a piece from an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the song turns round; the opening A stays put in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the standard term for an elaborate solo song sung by a single voice within an opera.

clue.text: Passing appreciation for charm

blocks.note: passing is a euphemism for death, one's end
as in having an ear for music, an appreciation of it

explanation.surface: Someone momentarily admiring another person's charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' reads as an adjective meaning brief, but it is the noun for dying, an end.
explanation.definitionFit: To win someone's affection or make yourself liked is to charm them, both used as verbs here.

clue.text: Complaint when money box originally up-ended

indicators.note: what something was originally is how it began, so only its opening letter is wanted
turning something end over end in a down entry makes it read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a fee is a sum of money paid for a service
the initial letter of box

explanation.surface: A grumble when a piggy bank has been tipped over to get the coins out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money box' looks like one thing, a piggy bank, but the two words give separate pieces: FEE then B, read upwards as BEEF.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is informal slang for a grievance or grumble, as in 'what's your beef?'

clue.text: Mountain guide in new phase touring capital of Romania

indicators.note: the capital letter of a word is its initial, so only the start of the name is taken
making something new remakes it, so these letters come out in a fresh order
a touring party goes all round a place, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the first letter of Romania

explanation.surface: A mountain guide begins a fresh stage of their career by touring Bucharest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital of Romania' tempts a solver toward Bucharest, but it means only the letter R, which sits inside the rearranged PHASE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sherpa people of Nepal are famed as Himalayan porters, and the name is used for any expert high-altitude climbing guide.

clue.text: Traditionalist sad after withdrawal of Conservative from temporary peace agreement

indicators.note: when something is withdrawn it is pulled out, so one letter leaves the word
one thing coming after another fixes the order, so the first-named piece goes second

blocks.note: a truce is a temporary halt to fighting
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
feeling blue means feeling sad

explanation.surface: A traditional politician is unhappy that the Conservatives have pulled out of a ceasefire deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the C from TRUCE to leave TRUE, then add BLUE. Blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative Party, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: True blue describes someone staunchly loyal and conservative, especially a dyed-in-the-wool Tory supporter in Britain.

clue.text: Not going anywhere without a proposal?

blocks.note: a motion is a formal proposal put to a meeting
-less is the suffix meaning without

explanation.surface: A relationship stalls because nobody has popped the question.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a marriage proposal, but the proposal is a debating motion; 'without' supplies the suffix, so the word order is reversed into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that stays completely still and stationary is not moving towards any place at all.

clue.text: Bag snatched by wild thing, dark-haired girl

indicators.note: something snatched is held in another's grasp, so one piece ends up inside the other

blocks.note: a brute is a savage beast
to net is to bag or catch

explanation.surface: A dark-haired girl has her handbag grabbed by a savage creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bag' reads as a handbag noun but stands for a net, a bag of mesh.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the usual term for a woman or girl whose hair is dark brown.

clue.text: Princess in a star, performing

indicators.note: a performance puts things through their paces, so these letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A royal princess appears on stage as the star of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a star' looks like stage billing, but its seven letters are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsarina was a Russian royal, the wife or daughter of a tsar, so loosely a princess or empress.

clue.text: Public school trouble!

blocks.note: first meaning: a famous fee-paying school in north-west London
second meaning: to distress or torment someone

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a public school is a private, fee-charging one; Harrow is among the best known. The exclamation suggests trouble at the school.
explanation.definitionFit: The school is a proper name; as a verb the word means to distress deeply, from the farm tool that tears the soil.

clue.text: Snapper arrived with tailless ray

indicators.note: with no tail, the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: came is the past tense of come, to arrive
taken as written

explanation.surface: A snapper fish turns up alongside a ray that has lost its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snapper' and 'ray' make the reader think of fish; the snapper is something that takes snaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A snapper is a person or device that takes snapshots, so a photographic device fits.

clue.text: Make flier? Don’t bother!

blocks.note: to forge is to make by shaping metal
a tit is a small bird, a flier

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to produce a leaflet and is told not to trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a printed leaflet, but here it is a creature that flies.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dismissive phrases telling someone to drop the matter and not trouble themselves.

clue.text: Fool, man with piece of dialogue cut, his films were silent

indicators.note: something cut is shortened, so the word drops its last letter

blocks.note: a charlie is British slang for a fool
a chap is a man
a line is a single piece of an actor's dialogue

explanation.surface: A film comedian plays the fool, his speeches edited out, so his films had no sound.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a 'right charlie' is a fool. LINE loses its E.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaplin was the great comic star of the silent cinema era, making many films without spoken dialogue.

clue.text: Unlucky, that dairy product’s not spreadable!

definitions.note: the answer is an exclamation of sympathy rather than an adjective

blocks.note: first meaning: a British expression of mock sympathy for bad luck
second meaning: a firm cheese, like cheddar, that won't spread

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation is old-fashioned British slang, often said with little real sympathy, meaning 'tough luck'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'hard cheese' is like saying 'tough luck', and a literal firm cheese such as Parmesan cannot be spread on bread.

clue.text: Stick Christmas lights in new grotto, first of all

indicators.note: the first of all the words means the opening letter of each one

blocks.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Someone attaching festive fairy lights inside a freshly built Santa's grotto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' is the definition at the front; every word after it up to the indicator gives one initial.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere firmly to something, as tape or a burr does, is to stick to it.

clue.text: Network, good and clear

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to rid is to clear of something

explanation.surface: A broadcasting network has a good, clear signal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' reads as an adjective, but it is the verb, as in clearing a house of mice.
explanation.definitionFit: A grid is a lattice of crossing lines, and also the national electricity supply system of cables.

clue.text: Windy plain in which anything’s sheltered

indicators.note: what is sheltered sits inside a protective cover, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: dry means plain or unadorned, as in dry toast or dry humour
aught is an old word for anything

explanation.surface: An exposed, windswept plain where nothing finds cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like the flat land of the surface but is the adjective, giving DRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A draughty room or place is one where cold currents of air blow through, so it is windy.

clue.text: A girl in the wrong place

definitions.note: the answer is an adverb or adjective, matching the phrase

blocks.note: taken as written
the title for an unmarried young woman, used to mean a girl

explanation.surface: A girl who has turned up somewhere she shouldn't be.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about a lost girl, but 'in the wrong place' is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something amiss is out of order, faulty or not as it should be, so wrongly placed or awry.

clue.text: Trick with void serial number

indicators.note: a void thing is emptied, so only the shell of the word, its outside letters, remains

blocks.note: the outside letters of serial
eight is a number

explanation.surface: A con involving a cancelled serial number on a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serial number' reads as one phrase, but it splits: the emptied word and then any number.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight, as in sleight of hand, is a deceptive skill or piece of trickery.

clue.text: Flat in Stevenage

indicators.note: what is in a word lies within its letters, so the answer is found inside it

blocks.note: letters two to five of the town's name

explanation.surface: An apartment in Stevenage, a new town north of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like a noun for an apartment; it is the adjective, meaning level.
explanation.definitionFit: An even surface is smooth and level, the same as a flat one.

clue.text: Flute changes a psalm remarkably, trilling finally coming in

indicators.note: done remarkably means done in an unusual way, so the letters take an unexpected order
what comes finally is at the end, so only the last letter is taken
something coming in enters, so one letter goes inside the rest

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the final letter of trilling

explanation.surface: A flute player alters a psalm, with trills added at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flute' suggests the musical instrument, matching the psalm and trilling; it is the tall glass. 'Changes' is fodder, not an indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A flute is a tall, narrow-stemmed glass designed for serving sparkling wine such as champagne.

clue.text: A reply that’s confused actor

indicators.note: something confused is mixed up, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor gives a muddled answer, perhaps having forgotten the lines.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the opening two words together, A and REPLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A player is an old word for someone who acts in plays, as in Shakespeare's travelling players.

clue.text: Character, someone leasing property?

blocks.note: first meaning: a single symbol of the alphabet
second meaning: one who lets out a house, read as let plus -er

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: one who lets, a word nobody normally uses.
explanation.definitionFit: A written symbol such as A or B is a character, and a landlord renting out a flat is one who lets it.

clue.text: Debauched regent, as rank

indicators.note: debauched means corrupted, so the letters are perverted out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dissolute prince regent, as foul as can be, recalling the debauched Regency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' seems to be an adjective meaning foul, describing the regent; it is the noun, a military grade.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant is a military or police officer grade, above corporal, so it is one rank.

clue.text: Some pretty petty sort!

indicators.note: some of something is only part of it, so the answer is a portion of the letters

blocks.note: the end of pretty joined to the start of petty

explanation.surface: Describing someone as a rather small-minded sort of person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty' reads as an adverb meaning fairly, and 'sort' as a person, but 'sort' is the definition and those words just hold the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A sort and a type are both a kind or category of things grouped together.

clue.text: Devastated when stuffing knocked out?

definitions.note: phrase used as a past participle, as is the answer

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for bitterly disappointed
second meaning: with the insides removed, as a fish is cleaned

explanation.walkthrough: Gutted is everyday British slang for crushed by disappointment; 'having the stuffing knocked out of you' is the same feeling, read here literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A gutted fish or building has had its innards removed, and a gutted person feels utterly crushed emotionally.

clue.text: Mark‘s call to dog having released lead

indicators.note: letting go of the lead lets the front go, so the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: the command given to a dog to retrieve a ball or stick

explanation.surface: Someone named Mark shouts to his dog after letting it off its leash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' suggests a dog's leash, fitting the scene, but in wordplay it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch something is to engrave or cut lines into a surface, which marks it.

clue.text: Fly set to buzz about twice!

indicators.note: moved about means shifted around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
twice means the same three letters are used a second time, rearranged the same way

explanation.surface: An insect primed to buzz around repeatedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' could be a verb, but it names the insect; the rearranged three letters are written out two times.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsetse is an African biting insect, a species of fly that spreads sleeping sickness.

clue.text: Little girl and niece played card game

indicators.note: something played is toyed with, so the letters are moved about freely

blocks.note: Pat is a short form of the girl's name Patricia
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A small girl and her niece spent the afternoon at a game of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little girl' means a shortened girl's name, not a child. 'Played' looks like the main verb but rearranges the relative.
explanation.definitionFit: Patience is the British name for solitaire, a one-player game laid out with a pack of cards.
